title: The same condition twice
summary: How a repeated condition in an if and else if chain can compile and run while sending values to the wrong branch.
objectives: Explain why an else if condition is checked only after the earlier if condition is false.
Trace an if and else if chain to predict which branch runs.
Find a repeated condition that makes a branch impossible to reach.
Correct a repeated condition by checking what values each branch should handle.

blocks.text: An if and else if chain checks conditions in order. Each later condition is checked only when the earlier conditions were false. A common copy-and-paste mistake is to repeat a condition instead of changing it. The program can compile and run without a warning, but it can choose the wrong branch.

bad.title: The middle case repeats the first condition

good.title: Each case checks a different range

blocks.note: For a score of `72`, the repeated `score >= 80` is false both times, so the bad version prints `Needs more practice`. The corrected condition, `score >= 60`, is true, so it prints `Pass`. Both snippets compile; the mistake appears when they run.

sections.title: Why the second condition cannot help

blocks.text: A condition is a test that produces `true` or `false`. With the same unchanged `score`, the test `score >= 80` has the same result each time. The second test is reached only if the first one was false. So if the second test is identical, it must be false too.

blocks.caption: The repeated test is reached only after the first test was false
blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A{score >= 80} -->|yes| B[Print Top mark]
  A -->|no| C{score >= 80 again}
  C -->|yes| D[Print Pass]
  C -->|no| E[Print Needs more practice]

blocks.title: Ask what the earlier test already proved
blocks.text: When the first test `score >= 80` is false, the score is below `80`. Testing `score >= 80` again cannot make it true. The next condition needs to describe a different case.

sections.title: Trace it one test at a time

blocks.text: Trace the bad version with `score = 72`. Write down each test in the order Java checks it. Stop when a branch runs.

blocks.caption: Tracing the repeated condition with score = 72
rows: Because the first test was false, check the `else if` condition `score >= 80`

blocks.text: The middle branch is skipped. With the corrected condition `score >= 60`, the second test is true for `72`, and the program prints `Pass`.
In each example, first ask which inputs should reach each branch. Then compare those intended cases with the conditions in the code.

bad.title: Example 1: a repeated score condition

good.title: Fix: use the pass threshold

blocks.note: The first branch handles scores of `80` or more. The second should handle scores below `80` but at least `60`, so its condition is `score >= 60`. Both programs compile; only the corrected one gives the intended result for `72`.

bad.title: Example 2: a repeated menu choice

good.title: Fix: check for choice 2

blocks.note: The first branch checks whether `choice == 1`. If that test is false, checking `choice == 1` again cannot select a different choice. The second branch needs to check `choice == 2`.

blocks.title: A quick way to check a branch
items: Name one example value that should reach the branch.
Check each earlier condition using that value.
Check the branch condition. If an earlier identical test was false, this one cannot be true.

blocks.text: Repeated conditions can look different in real code. The key question is still the same: can this branch be reached after the earlier conditions have failed?

good.title: A different choice for each branch

blocks.note: If `choice == 1` is false, the same test in the `else if` is false too. Use the value meant for the second choice.
A boolean holds `true` or `false`. If `ready` is false, the second test of `ready` is also false, so that branch never runs. Since there are only two cases here, an `else` handles the false case.

blocks.caption: Branch results for the sample scores 55, 65, 75 and 85

blocks.text: The chart counts the four sample scores in each output category. With the repeated condition, no score reaches `Pass`. The corrected conditions put `65` and `75` in that category.

blocks.question: What does this code print when `number` is `4`?
blocks.explanation: The first test `number == 4` is true, so Java runs that branch and skips the rest of the chain. The code compiles.

blocks.question: The first test `temperature < 0` was false. Can an `else if` with the same test `temperature < 0` be true?
options: Yes, every `else if` gets a fresh value
No, the same test on the unchanged value is false
Only if the program is compiled again
The condition is not a boolean
blocks.explanation: For the same unchanged `temperature`, the same comparison has the same result. If the first test was false, the repeated test is false too.

blocks.question: A program should print `Small` for values below `10` and `Large` for values of `10` or more. Which condition belongs in the `else if`?
blocks.explanation: The first branch handles values below `10`. The remaining values are `10` or more, so `value >= 10` describes the second case.
